story.headline: US shares tumbled on new tariff plans and a chip sell-off, erasing the dollar's early gain from strong US data. Gold won back its whole drop, and oil jumped about 3% on Gulf attack claims.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike stays all but certain, and the Fed's Beige Book survey gave no reason to doubt it. The stock slide made traders a little less sure about more hikes after that. Canada's central bank looks set to hike again, which is lifting the loonie.
reads.growth: The US economy is still running hot, with growth revised up sharply and layoffs rare. Germany barely grew over the same months. That gap favors the dollar, though the stock slide is a new risk to US spending.
reads.inflation: US core inflation edged up again in October, and firms in the Fed's survey said costs keep rising, with tariffs among the causes. Australian inflation is also climbing. Both keep their central banks from easing.
reads.risk: US shares fell hard as chip stocks kept sliding and the US proposed new tariffs, and money moved into US government bonds. The Swiss franc gained most, and gold won back its whole morning drop. The Aussie and kiwi held up better than feared once the dollar weakened.
reads.tot: Oil jumped on claims of attacks on a Saudi refinery and on tankers near Hormuz, which helps the Canadian dollar and hurts oil importers like Japan and the euro area. Gold's recovery takes some pressure off Australia's export earnings.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Heavy bets against the loonie leave room for a fast unwind if Canadian hike bets keep growing.
reads.fiscal: The US proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, hardest on China and Southeast Asia, but nothing takes effect before early 2027. For Europe, Japan and Switzerland the rates sit near caps in existing deals. France's debts remain a weight on the euro, with S&P due to review its credit rating on Friday.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Traders fully expect a quarter-point hike on December 9, with another in January a little more likely than not.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike all but certain. January: another hike a little more likely than not.
fed.why: US growth was revised up to a 4.3% pace and core inflation rose to 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% goal. The Fed's Beige Book survey on Wednesday, November 25 found steady growth and stubborn price rises.
fed.watch: Whether the slide in US shares deepens enough to make the Fed more careful after December. The decision is December 9, with new forecasts from officials.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October. Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, November 24 the bank may need to act sooner, and traders now see a December hike as likely.
boc.why: Macklem warned the oil shock will keep prices sticky and said the bank was too slow to spot lasting inflation after the pandemic. Oil's jump on Wednesday, November 25 adds to that worry.
boc.watch: Canada's third-quarter growth on Monday, November 30, the jobs report on Friday, December 4, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, but a jump in shop sales in the third quarter strengthens the case for one.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is about double its goal, but the euro sits near its weakest in about 19 months as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Slow German growth, weak factories and France's debts limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: The accounts of the October meeting on Thursday, November 26 at 6:30 AM CT, and S&P's review of France's credit rating on Friday, November 27. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Inflation is above its 2% goal, but the dollar still trades near 159 yen because US rates keep rising faster.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2%, and prices firms charge each other for services are rising fast. But the bank's own core inflation measure cooled in October, one reason some, such as JPMorgan, see December as closer to a coin flip.
boj.watch: Tokyo's November inflation on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Inflation jumped to 4.9% in October, which ended bets on a cut soon, though job losses argue against another hike.
rba.priced: December: hold expected. Cuts in 2027 now look less likely.
rba.why: Inflation is well above the bank's 2–3% target and rising, but job losses and shrinking business activity argue for patience. That leaves the bank holding, with the risk now leaning toward another hike rather than a cut.
rba.watch: Australian business investment on Wednesday, November 25 at 6:30 PM CT and Australia's third-quarter growth on Wednesday, December 2. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, and markets lean toward another hike on December 17. Its leaders sounded split before lawmakers on Wednesday, November 25.
boe.why: Governor Andrew Bailey said inflation may peak lower if energy prices hold, while policymaker Catherine Mann wants more hikes sooner. High fuel costs still keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal.
boe.watch: The Financial Stability Report on Thursday, November 26 at 4:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Further falls in stock markets or Gulf flare-ups that send money into the franc, and the new US tariff plans for Swiss goods. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight, and markets lean toward another Bank of England hike in December. It still trades near a one-year low against the dollar.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Hot inflation makes cuts less likely, but nervous markets and new US tariffs on China keep it near its lowest this year.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm dairy prices help, but doubts over a December rate hike and nervous markets keep it near a 17-year low.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates and a fast-growing economy support it, while large budget deficits weigh. It slipped as US shares slid, though a December Fed hike is still fully expected.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Germany's economy is barely growing and France's debts hold the euro back. It trades near $1.10, not far above its weakest in about 19 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board, because recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. A likely December Bank of Canada hike and firmer oil lifted it to a two-week high against the US dollar.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike and the threat of Japan stepping in keep the dollar just under 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains when fear in markets sends money its way, as it did when US shares slid.
